newsitem.title: USA: Death penalty sought for D.C. police killers.
newsitem.headline: Death penalty sought for D.C. police killers.

text.p: A bill to impose the federal death penalty for murdering a District of Columbia police officer was introduced Monday by Republican Sen. Kay Bailey Hutchison of Texas.

Hutchison named the bill for Brian Gibson, the Washington police officer who was murdered last Wednesday while he sat in his squad car in front of a night club. A suspect was arrested but he can be sentenced at most to life in prison if he is found guilty because the city does not have a death penalty.
"We cannot and will not tolerate a situation in which officers of the law in our nation's capital can be callously slain while protecting the rest of us," Hutchison said.
Most of the District of Columbia's laws are made by an elected city council, but Congress provides much of the city's budget and has oversight authority over its government.
Hutchison said Congress had a duty to act to protect the nation's capital city, which is in serious financial trouble and plagued by high rates of murder and violent crime.

"I think everyone is concerned about what is happening in the District of Columbia," she said. "I do believe if you send a strong signal they (potential murderers) are going to think twice about committing a capital crime."
Many Washington police officers are calling for the federal government to take over the force because they are so short of money and resources.
Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott, a Mississippi Republican, said Friday Congress and the White House had to take strong action to save the city because conditions were deteriorating rapidly.
Washington residents strongly rejected a referendum calling for the death penalty four years ago. The death penalty is legal in 38 of the 50 states.

Murderers of federal law officers, such as U.S. Capitol police or White House guards, can be executed under federal law. However, the federal government has not executed anyone for more than 30 years.
